title: Bitkey (Block, Inc.): 2-of-3 multisig keys, seedless recovery, inheritance, and privacy
plain:
Bitkey is a self-custody bitcoin wallet from Block, Inc., the company behind Square and Cash App, that replaces the traditional seed phrase with a 2-of-3 multisig design. Instead of one master key, three keys protect the funds: one generated and stored on the hardware device, one held in the mobile app, and one held on Bitkey's servers. Any two of the three keys are required to move money. Because the user holds two of the keys (the hardware key and the app key), funds can always be moved without Bitkey's participation, and Bitkey cannot move funds on its own.

Each key has a distinct job. The hardware key is generated and stored completely offline, is protected by a secure enclave, and requires the owner's fingerprint to unlock. The app key lives in the mobile app and as an encrypted backup in the user's own cloud account (Google Drive or iCloud); Bitkey's servers can never access that backup, and the app key alone cannot sign payments above a set limit without the hardware. The server key, held by Bitkey in an AWS Nitro Enclave, can co-sign app-key payments up to the set daily limit if the user opts in to 'Transfer without hardware', and it participates in recovery, but it cannot move money by itself and cannot authorize recovery without the user's hardware or app key.

Because there is no seed phrase, recovery works through key replacement rather than phrase restoration. If you lose your phone, download the app on a new phone, sign in to your cloud account, unlock the hardware device, and tap to decrypt the encrypted app-key backup. Only the unlocked physical device can decrypt that backup. If the hardware is lost, the app key and the server key are used to pair a new hardware device, after a 7-day security waiting period with notifications sent by SMS, email, and the app; a network fee applies when funds are swept to the new wallet. If the cloud backup is lost as well, the hardware key plus the server key can still recover the funds, but a new wallet with three new keys must be created to sweep the funds into, again after the 7-day waiting period. If both the phone and the hardware are lost, Recovery Contacts — people you know and trust — verify your identity with a shared code and help create a new encrypted backup of the mobile key; they never gain access to your keys, balance, or transactions. If Bitkey itself becomes unavailable, the Emergency Exit Kit, a PDF generated at setup and stored in your cloud account, contains the encrypted app key; the hardware device decrypts it over NFC, and open-source software can then coordinate signing with both of your keys.

Bitkey also offers an inheritance feature. A beneficiary is added in the app, and the beneficiary needs their own Bitkey app and hardware device. Until a claim is processed, the beneficiary has no access to keys, bitcoin, or wallet information. A claim starts a 6-month security waiting period during which Bitkey attempts to notify the primary user by push, email, and SMS, and the primary user can cancel the claim while it is active. After the waiting period, Bitkey delivers the app key — which was encrypted at setup so that only the beneficiary can decrypt it — and co-signs with the server key.

On privacy, Bitkey requires no KYC, stores no biometrics, and has no customer support staff authorizing actions; cryptographic keys verify actions instead. Orders can be shipped to third-party pickup points such as FedEx locations, Dollar General, Albertsons, Kroger, and about 9,000 Walgreens stores in the United States, and paying with bitcoin plus a pickup point requires only an email address and a pickup name. A technique called Chain Code Delegation, co-developed by Bitkey engineers as a bitcoin improvement proposal, lets the third-party keyholder participate in recovery and spending limits without learning your unrelated transactions or balances, though it still sees transactions that require its participation.

Keep the honest limitations in view. Do not assume Bitkey is trustless self-custody: the server key makes it a collaborative design, and you rely on Block, Inc. to operate its key honestly. The product costs money ($250 USD at the time of this snapshot), and everyday use, recovery, and inheritance depend on Block's app and servers remaining available. Keep access to the email address and phone number tied to your wallet, because recovery and inheritance notifications are sent through those channels. Do not treat email and SMS notifications as guaranteed, because losing those channels means missing delay-period warnings. Store the Emergency Exit Kit PDF in your cloud account and keep access to it, because it is your path to your funds if Bitkey becomes unavailable. If you intend to use the inheritance feature, add a beneficiary in the app and make sure they have their own Bitkey app and hardware device. Do not rely on the inheritance feature for immediate access: the claim includes a 6-month waiting period, and until it is processed the beneficiary has no access to keys, bitcoin, or wallet information. Do not enable 'Transfer without hardware' unless you accept that the server key can co-sign app payments up to your set daily limit.
technical:
Bitkey combines a cold signer (the hardware device, which holds keys offline, never needs to be online to sign, and does not know the wallet balance) with hot-wallet flexibility (the mobile app); a signer alone is not enough, because wallet software is required to interact with the bitcoin network, and a purely hot wallet keeps its only signing key on an internet-connected device. The 2-of-3 multisig construction means no single key can move funds, which raises the cost and technical bar compared with singlesig, where knowledge of a seed phrase alone can suffice. The vendor's stated rationale for dropping the seed phrase is that a 12- or 24-word backup is a single point of failure that is as easy for anyone else to use as it is for the owner. The Bitkey mobile app is open source. Block, Inc. open-sourced Subzero, an HSM-based custodial solution, in 2020; it is used for Cash App customer balances and Block's treasury, which is relevant context for the company's operational track record. Customer server keys reside in an AWS Nitro Enclave, a hardware-isolated secure execution environment, and code deployments require approval from multiple engineers in a dedicated deployer group with hardware-token authentication. The hardware key is generated and stored completely offline and protected by a secure enclave; a singlesig wallet can be breached with a PIN or passphrase plus physical access, while spending with Bitkey requires biometrics and a second key. The app key is useless without the unlocked hardware device, and the app can set security and spending rules and start recovery but cannot sign payments over the set limit without hardware. The hardware measures 66 x 60 x 13.6 mm, weighs 79 g, has a Corian solid-surface body with an OLED touchscreen, a biometric fingerprint sensor, NFC, USB-C, and a battery rated for up to one year.

The Emergency Exit Kit is a PDF generated at setup that contains the encrypted app key and is stored in the user's cloud account; the hardware device communicates with third-party software over NFC to decrypt it, a QR code in the kit links to open-source software that automates creating and signing with both user-held keys, and users may build their own, so the owner always controls two private keys without relying on Block. Recovery Contacts hold their own encryption key rather than the owner's spending key, so their participation verifies identity without granting them wallet access. During inheritance, Bitkey holds the encrypted app key but cannot unlock it; after the 6-month waiting period it delivers the encrypted key and co-signs with the server key, which avoids the pitfalls of seed-phrase sharing (insecure and reveals balances) and of written instructions that can be lost or misunderstood.

On privacy engineering, no KYC is required and no biometrics are stored; actions are verified by cryptographic keys rather than by customer support staff. Chain Code Delegation, a bitcoin improvement co-authored by Bitkey engineers that any multisig or collaborative provider can adopt, lets a cosigner participate in recovery and spending limits without learning unrelated transactions or balances, though the third-party keyholder still sees transactions that require its participation. Recovery co-signing gives the server a momentary view into the wallet balance, which Bitkey states is not logged or stored, and the company says it is working on a feature that would let anyone verify that its servers do not log. Compared with most collaborative-custody providers, which require full KYC and/or biometric support approval, Bitkey's remaining privacy exposure is mainly the e-commerce platform, shipping, and communications channels; hardware shipping requires address and billing information, while paying with bitcoin avoids billing information and using a pickup point avoids a home address.

warnings: Collaborative-custody element: Bitkey's server holds one of the three keys, so the user relies on Block, Inc. to operate that key honestly and to keep its infrastructure secure; this is not fully independent self-custody.
Paid, company-dependent product: the hardware cost $250 USD at the snapshot date, and everyday use, recovery, and inheritance features depend on Block's app and servers remaining available.

Notification-channel reliance: recovery and inheritance delay periods notify via email, SMS, and push; losing access to those channels can mean missing warnings, including the chance to cancel an inheritance claim.

Opt-in spending without hardware: when 'Transfer without hardware' is enabled, the server key co-signs app payments up to a set daily limit, weakening the property that every spend requires the hardware device.

Snapshot-dated facts: pricing, waiting-period lengths, pickup-point availability, and feature details reflect the vendor's learning hub as captured 2026-10-11 and may change; verify against current Bitkey documentation.
